source_text: Σκοπῶμεν δὲ οὕτως. Εἰ πᾶσα ἀπιστία μὴ προχείρως καὶ κατά τινα δόξαν ἄκριτον ἐγγινομένη τισίν, ἀλλὰ μετά τινος αἰτίας ἰσχυρᾶς καὶ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἀσφαλείας· τότε γὰρ τὸν εἰκότα σώζει λόγον, ὅταν αὐτὸ τὸ πρᾶγμα περὶ οὖ ἀπιστοῦσιν ἄπιστον εἶναι δοκῇ· τὸ γάρ τοι τοῖς οὐκ οὖσιν ἀπίστοις ἀπιστεῖν ἀνθρώπων ἔργον οὐχ ὑγιαινούσῃ κρίσει περὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν χρωμένων. Οὐκοῦν χρὴ καὶ τοὺς περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἀπιστοῦντας ἢ διαποροῦντας μὴ πρὸς τὸ δοκοῦν αὐτοῖς ἀκρίτως καὶ τὸ τοῖς ἀκολάστοις κεχαρισμένον τὴν περὶ ταύτης ἐκφέρειν γνώμην, ἀλλ᾿ ἢ μηδεμιᾶς αἰτίας ἐξάπτειν τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένεσιν (ὃ δὴ καὶ λίαν ἐστὶν εὐεξέλεγκτον), ἢ τῷ θεῷ τὴν τῶν ὄντων ἀνατιθέντας αἰτίαν εἰς τὴν τοῦδε τοῦ δόγματος ἀποβλέπειν ὑπόθεσιν, καὶ διὰ ταύτης δεικνύναι τὴν ἀνάστασιν οὐδαμόθεν ἔχουσαν τὸ πιστόν. Τοῦτο δὲ ποιήσουσιν, ἐὰν δεῖξαι δυνηθῶσιν ἢ ἀδύνατον ὂν τῷ θεῷ ἢ ἀβούλητον τὰ νεκρωθέντα τῶν σωμάτων ἢ καὶ πάντη διαλυθέντα πάλιν ἑνῶσαι καὶ συναγαγεῖν πρὸς τὴν τῶν αὐτῶν ἀνθρώπων σύστασιν. Ἐὰν δὲ τοῦτο μὴ δύνωνται, παυσάσθωσαν τῆς ἀθέου ταύτης ἀπιστίας καὶ τοῦ βλασφημεῖν ἃ μὴ θέμις· ὅτι γὰρ οὔτε τὸ ἀδύνατον λέγοντες ἀληθεύουσιν οὔτε τὸ ἀβούλητον, ἐκ τῶν ῥηθησομένων γενήσεται φανερόν. Τὸ ἀδύνατόν τινι γινώσκεται κατ᾿ ἀλήθειαν τοιοῦτον ἢ ἐκ τοῦ μὴ γινώσκειν τὸ γενησόμενον, ἢ ἐκ τοῦ δύναμιν ἀρκοῦσαν μὴ ἔχειν πρὸς τὸ ποιῆσαι καλῶς τὸ ἐγνωσμένον. Ὅ τε γὰρ ἀγνοῶν τι τῶν γενέσθαι δεόντων οὐκ ἂν οὔτ᾿ ἐγχειρῆσαι οὔτε ποιῆσαι τὸ παράπαν δυνηθείη ὅπερ ἀγνοεῖ· ὅ τε γινώσκων καλῶς τὸ ποιηθησόμενον, καὶ πόθεν γένοιτ᾿ ἂν καὶ πῶς, δύναμιν δὲ ἢ μηδ᾿ ὅλως ἔχων πρὸς τὸ ποιῆσαι τὸ γινωσκόμενον ἢ μὴ ἀρκοῦσαν ἔχων, οὐκ ἂν ἐγχειρήσειε τὴν ἀρχήν, εἰ σωφρονοίη καὶ τὴν ἰδίαν ἐπισκέψαιτο δύναμιν, ἐγχειρήσας δὲ ἀπερισκέπτως οὐκ ἂν ἐπιτελέσειε τὸ δόξαν. Ἀλλ᾿ οὔτε ἀγνοεῖν τὸν θεὸν δυνατὸν τῶν ἀναστησομένων σωμάτων τὴν φύσιν κατά τε μέρος ὅλον καὶ μόριον, οὔτε μὴν ὅποι χωρεῖ τῶν λυομένων ἕκαστον, καὶ ποῖον τῶν στοιχείων μέρος δέδεκται τὸ λυθὲν καὶ χωρῆσαν πρὸς τὸ συγγενές, κἂν πάνυ παρ᾿ ἀνθρώποις ἀδιάκριτον εἶναι δοκῇ τὸ τῷ παντὶ πάλιν προσφυῶς ἡνωμένον. Ὦι γὰρ οὐκ ἠγνόητο πρὸ τῆς οἰκείας ἑκάστου συστάσεως οὔτε τῶν γενησομένων στοιχείων ἡ φύσις ἐξ ὧν τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων σώματα, οὔτε τὰ μέρη τούτων ἐξ ὦν ἤμελλεν λήψεσθαι τὸ δόξαν πρὸς τὴν τοῦ ἀνθρωπείου σώματος σύστασιν, εὔδηλον ὡς οὐδὲ μετὰ τὸ διαλυθῆναι τὸ πᾶν ἀγνοηθήσεται ποῦ κεχώρηκεν ἕκαστον ὦν εἴληφε πρὸς τὴν ἑκάστου συμπλήρωσιν. ὅσον μὶν γὰρ κατὰ τὴν νῦν κρατοῦσαν παρ᾿ ἡμῖν τῶν πραγμάτων τάξιν καὶ τὴν ἐφ᾿ ἑτέρων κρίσιν, μεῖζον τὸ τὰ μὴ γενόμενα προγινώσκειν· ὅσον δὲ πρὸς τὴν ἀξίαν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τὴν τούτου σοφίαν, ἀμφότερα κατὰ φύσιν, καὶ ῥᾴδιον ἐπ᾿ ἴσης τῷ τὰ μὴ γενόμενα προγινώσκειν τὸ καὶ διαλυθέντα γινώσκειν.
pass_a_gloss: We consider thus. If every unbelief is not approaching rashly and according to some unexamined opinion, but with some strong reason and the safety according to truth; then indeed it saves the reasonable account, when the thing itself about which they disbelieve seems to be unbelievable; for to disbelieve the things that are not among the unbelieving people is a work of men not using healthy judgment about the truth. Therefore, it is necessary also for those disbelieving or doubting about the resurrection not to bring forth their opinion about it rashly and unexamined, as the things pleasing to the intemperate, but either to attribute the cause of human generation to no reason (which is very much open to criticism), or to attribute the cause of existing things to God and to look to the hypothesis of this doctrine, and through this to show that the resurrection has no trustworthy basis. They will do this, if they can show that it is either impossible for God or unwilling for God to reunite and gather again the dead bodies or even the things completely dissolved. But if they cannot do this, let them stop this ungodly unbelief and blaspheming the things that are not lawful; for it will become clear from the things that will be said that they are not speaking the truth, neither about the impossible nor about the unwilling. The impossible is known to someone as such either from not knowing the thing that will happen or from not having sufficient power to do well the thing known. For the one who is ignorant of some of the things that must happen would not be able to undertake or do at all what he is ignorant of; the one who knows well the thing to be done and from where and how it will happen, but has either no power or insufficient power to do the known thing, would not undertake the beginning, if he were sane and examined his own power, and if he undertook it without examination, he would not complete the thing as expected. But God is not able to be ignorant of the nature of the bodies to be resurrected, either in whole or in part, nor where each of the dissolved things goes, and what part of the elements the dissolved thing has been attached to and gone to its kind, even if it seems to men to be completely indistinguishable what is reunited and joined again to the whole. For it was not unknown to God before the creation of each thing, either the nature of the elements from which the human bodies would be, or the parts of these from which the human body would receive its form, it is clear that even after the whole is dissolved, it will not be unknown where each of the things that were taken for the completion of each has gone. For as much as according to the present order of things among us and the judgment about others, it is greater to know the things that have not happened; as much as according to the worth of God and his wisdom, both according to nature, it is equally easy to know the things that have not happened and to know the things that have been dissolved.
pass_b_english: We consider the matter this way. If unbelief does not arise rashly or from some unexamined opinion, but from a strong reason and the certainty that comes from truth, then it preserves a reasonable account—specifically when the thing disbelieved actually appears to be incredible. For it is the act of people who do not exercise sound judgment about truth to disbelieve things that are not genuinely unbelievable. Therefore, those who disbelieve or doubt the resurrection must not put forward their opinion about it rashly and without examination, as if it were something pleasing to the intemperate. Instead, they must either attribute the cause of human generation to no reason at all—which is very much open to refutation—or attribute the cause of existing things to God, look to the hypothesis of this doctrine, and through it demonstrate that the resurrection has no trustworthy basis whatsoever.

They will accomplish this if they can show that it is either impossible for God or contrary to his will to reunite and gather again the bodies that have died, or even those that have completely dissolved, and restore them to the composition of the same human beings. But if they cannot do this, let them cease this ungodly unbelief and stop blaspheming what is not lawful to blaspheme. For it will become clear from what follows that they speak the truth neither about the impossible nor about the unwilling.

The impossible is truly known to someone in two ways: either from not knowing what will happen, or from not having sufficient power to do well what is known. For one who is ignorant of some of the things that must happen would not be able to undertake or accomplish at all what he is ignorant of. And one who knows well what is to be done, and from where and how it will happen, but has either no power at all or insufficient power to do the known thing, would not undertake the beginning if he were sane and examined his own power; and if he undertook it without examination, he would not complete the thing as expected.

But God cannot be ignorant of the nature of the bodies to be resurrected, whether in whole or in part. Nor can he be ignorant of where each of the dissolved things goes, and what part of the elements has received the dissolved thing and gone to its kindred element—even if it seems to men to be completely indistinguishable what is fittingly reunited and joined again to the whole. For before the creation of each thing, it was not unknown to God either the nature of the elements from which human bodies would be formed, or the parts of these from which the human body would receive its form. It is clear, therefore, that even after the whole is dissolved, it will not be unknown where each of the things taken for the completion of each body has gone.

For as far as the present order of things among us and our judgment about others are concerned, it is greater to know things that have not yet happened. But as far as the worth of God and his wisdom are concerned, both are according to nature and equally easy: to know the things that have not yet happened and to know the things that have been dissolved.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex conditional arguments and philosophical distinctions regarding impossibility and ignorance in the Greek text. Pass A preserves the clause structure and nuances of the Greek, while Pass B provides a fluent rendering that remains faithful to the source. All theological distinctions (e.g., the distinction between 'impossible' and 'unwilling') are maintained.
